video_title: NYT CEO Meredith Kopit Levien on Running a Media Brand in the Age of AI | Odd Lots
gist: New York Times CEO Meredith Kopit Levien walks Odd Lots through the economics of the NYT bundle (entry at roughly $1/week with engineered price step-ups, a 'get everybody under the demand curve' strategy), the company's two-track AI posture (a licensing deal with Amazon alongside active suits against OpenAI, Microsoft and Perplexity, backed by ~$2B of annual content spend and a 175-year corpus), and a costly push into video that has coincided with post-earnings stock weakness. She insists news journalism — not games or sports — is the most economically value-creating product, and that family control lets the company fund long-horizon bets while editors, not finance, decide coverage spend.

themes.theme: Bundle pricing and the demand curve

insights.claim: The New York Times prices to capture the entire demand curve — from discounted international games-only subscriptions at the low end up to shared family-plan bundles at the top — rather than optimizing a single price point.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Segmented pricing plus product-led value increases is the mechanism behind NYT ARPU growth; watch ARPU and bundle mix rather than raw subscriber adds.
insights.quote: our pricing strategy is meant to get everybody under the demand curve

insights.claim: Most New York Times subscribers enter the full news-and-lifestyle bundle at about a dollar a week, engage over time, and are then moved to a materially higher price at a designed 'pricing step-up point,' a sequence the CEO says has gone 'really, really well.'
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: The promo-to-full-price conversion ladder, not headline subscriber counts, is the real driver of revenue per user; deceleration in step-up conversion would be the first crack in the model.
insights.quote: most people buy our news title bundle or which is the whole thing at a dollar a week. And then over time they engage. And then over time they reach a pricing step up point and they come to a much higher price

insights.claim: The news-and-lifestyle bundle is explicitly the NYT 'hero product' because it carries the most value, making bundle attachment — not standalone news subs — the company's primary commercial objective.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Bundle penetration rate is the KPI that best predicts pricing power and churn resistance at NYT.

insights.claim: The Times refused the standard paywall trade-off, deliberately keeping large volumes of high-quality work free to sample while preserving enough 'gravity' behind the paywall — a calibration Levien says has been managed continuously for over a decade to seed 'the next million subscribers.'
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Explains why NYT paywall tightness oscillates; a hard paywall pivot would signal the top-of-funnel is broken.
insights.quote: we never accepted that we had to choose between having a lot of stuff widely available so that people could sample our work, and also enough value and gravity in the product so that people would pay

insights.claim: Levien argues the addressable market in news and in every NYT lifestyle vertical remains large and only early-penetrated, implying management sees no near-term saturation ceiling on subscriber growth.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Management is guiding investors away from a maturity narrative; any explicit TAM concession on a future call would be a meaningful shift in tone.
insights.quote: We think there's a huge market in news and in every one of our lifestyle products, huge market. We are still early in penetrating that market

insights.claim: The bundle upsell mechanism works through content FOMO in adjacent verticals — host Tracy Alloway, a non-sports consumer without the upgraded subscription, said World Cup coverage from The Athletic was the first time she felt she was missing out and agreed on air to upgrade.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Live-event sports moments are a demonstrable conversion trigger for bundle upgrades — a reason The Athletic's value shows up in news-sub economics rather than standalone sports revenue.

insights.claim: Levien frames a decade-long strategic priority of pulling audience relationships off third-party platforms and into direct NYT control, calling that migration part of why the Times succeeded.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Direct-relationship ownership is what insulates NYT from AI-era search and social referral collapse that is hitting referral-dependent publishers.
insights.quote: we've been keenly aware for the better part of a decade that the direction of travel from the platforms will be the we should be getting more and more of it into our own control

themes.theme: AI licensing, litigation, and publisher leverage

insights.claim: The New York Times is running a dual-track AI strategy: it has signed a licensing deal with Amazon while simultaneously litigating against OpenAI and Microsoft (roughly three years in) and Perplexity (sued last December).
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: NYT is deliberately setting a litigation floor to raise the price of the deals it does sign — a template for content-owner leverage and a live legal overhang for OpenAI, Microsoft and Perplexity.
insights.quote: We've done a deal. We have also, sued three companies were suing. It were two and a half years, maybe almost three now in to suing OpenAI and Microsoft. Three. We sued Perplexity last December.

insights.claim: Levien sets three explicit conditions for any AI licensing deal: it must be continuous with a sustainable, growing publisher business; it must give the publisher explicit permission-granting and control over all uses; and it must deliver sustainable, fair value exchange.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: A reusable term-sheet checklist for evaluating any publisher-AI deal; deals lacking use-level control are the ones NYT will litigate rather than sign.

insights.claim: The New York Times spent close to $2 billion last year producing roughly half a million works of content and has been producing at some scale for 175 years, a cost base Levien uses to argue the corpus is far more valuable than what AI companies currently pay for 'data.'
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: The hardest public number in the episode: ~$4,000 of production cost per work, a benchmark for pricing content licensing against AI-lab training budgets.
insights.quote: we spent like close to $2 billion last year producing half a million works of content, stories, photos, videos, expressive, creative work that required enormous resource to go make and human beings to go make

insights.claim: Levien argues that AI labs spending tens to hundreds of billions on talent, compute and power are underpaying for the journalism and creative work they call 'data,' framing content compensation as structurally mispriced relative to the rest of the AI capex stack.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: If content licensing repriced to even a small fraction of compute budgets, it becomes a material new revenue line for premium publishers and a new cost line for AI labs.
insights.quote: These companies, the LLMs are spending, you know, tens of billions of dollars, sometimes hundreds of billions of dollars on talent, on compute, on power. They should be spending the money that is sufficient value for exchange.

insights.claim: Levien characterizes the core grievance against AI companies as theft plus competitive substitution — they took content without permission or control and built products that compete with the publisher — which is why enforcement in court sits alongside dealmaking.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Frames the dispute as product substitution rather than pure copyright, which raises the potential damages and the likelihood NYT holds out for control terms.
insights.quote: these companies have stolen our stuff. They've used it without her permission or any kind of control, and they've built products that can compete with us

insights.claim: Tracy Alloway notes that other media organizations, including Bloomberg, have rejected flat licensing agreements in favor of usage-based fees from AI companies, indicating the industry has not converged on a compensation model.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Fragmented publisher pricing models mean AI labs can arbitrage between lump-sum and usage-based counterparties until a standard emerges.

insights.claim: The New York Times has a dedicated AI initiatives team in the newsroom that built a tool set to cluster and pattern-match the roughly 3 million pages of Epstein files released on a Friday night, enabling stories the following week that would otherwise have taken far longer.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Concrete proof that AI's near-term publisher ROI is document-scale investigative speed, not text generation — a capability advantage that compounds for large newsrooms over small ones.
insights.quote: The Epstein files dropped on a Friday night, and I think it was, like three, 3 million pages of documents.

insights.claim: The Times used AI to disprove the social-media consensus on the Sydney Sweeney jeans controversy, showing the outrage was first constructed by the right rather than by the left — an example of AI enabling stories that could not previously be reported.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: AI-powered narrative-provenance analysis is a defensible new journalism product category that independent one-person outlets cannot easily replicate.
insights.quote: the idea on social media was that it was like people on the left were outraged, the libs are outraged, and we actually used AI to prove that it was first a construction of the. Right.

insights.claim: Levien's favorite internal AI use case was sorting existing aerial imagery of tennis courts to count how many had been converted to pickleball courts, illustrating that computer vision over public data is now a routine investigative input.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Signals that the marginal cost of quantitative, data-derived features is falling fast, expanding the volume of differentiated content per journalist.
insights.quote: My favorite example is we were trying to convey this new trend in sport, and we used AI to sort through all this existing aerial imagery of tennis courts

insights.claim: Levien draws a firm line that high-quality independent journalism and creative work must remain human-led, while accepting AI for efficiency, accessibility, automated voice and translation — where she sees real opportunity as the technology improves.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: AI translation and automated voice are the most likely near-term international TAM expansion levers for NYT without proportional editorial cost.
insights.quote: the way we think about it today first is what's the work that should be human led? And I want to say high quality, independent journalism, human led, human led, creative stuff

insights.claim: The Times employs close to a thousand people in digital product development and about 3,000 journalists and content makers, and Levien expects the journalism headcount to keep growing as long as the company keeps succeeding — an explicitly anti-AI-displacement view for creative roles.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Rebuts the thesis that AI compresses publisher opex; NYT margin expansion is expected from revenue growth, not editorial headcount cuts.
insights.quote: we've got close to a thousand people doing digital product development in the New York Times, you know, 3000 journalists and people making content

insights.claim: Levien says token spend has become the standard question among CEOs — she is on another public company board and 'everyone is talking about this' — but argues nobody can credibly forecast it yet given evaluation and human-judgment overhead, so NYT has not turned it into a multi-year capital planning line.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Useful check on AI-inference demand models: large enterprise buyers are still in experimentation mode and not yet budgeting token spend as a durable line item.
insights.quote: I think it's going to be some time before anybody is going to give you a really credible answer to that question.

insights.claim: The Times has rolled out coding tools broadly across product development and marketing, indicating AI adoption at NYT is deepest in engineering and commercial functions rather than in editorial output.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Maps where AI seat-license revenue actually lands inside media companies: developer and marketing tooling, not newsroom writing tools.

insights.claim: Levien is not offended by AI drafting from field-reported inputs — the old reporter/writer split Henry Blodget described — provided technology increases the volume of actual reporting, which she defines as the irreducibly human act of going out and unearthing new information with sensitivity and judgment.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Defines the defensible moat for publishers as origination of information, not composition — the part of the value chain AI cannot commoditize.
insights.quote: am I offended by the idea that there are a bunch of things that tech, including generative AI, can do so that we can have more reporting? I'm not offended by that idea at all.

insights.claim: The New York Times newsroom has roughly a thousand more journalists than 13 years ago and holds the largest collection of journalists in its history even excluding The Athletic and Wirecutter, a scale Levien treats as the core competitive asset.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Headcount scale is the barrier to entry Levien is betting on; it is also the fixed cost that makes NYT unattractive to replicate and hard to unwind if growth stalls.
insights.quote: there are like a thousand more journalists in the New York Times newsroom today than when I got there 13 years ago

insights.claim: The NYT retention model is peer-and-infrastructure based rather than compensation based: journalists stay for the best editors, lawyers, security, graphics and photographers around them, with Jonathan Swan and Ezra Klein cited as evidence.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: If the moat is support infrastructure rather than pay, NYT's talent costs stay contained even as Substack economics improve — but the model self-selects against solo-brand stars.
insights.quote: The best journalists in their career at the top of their game, coming to do the best work of their careers, supported by the best editors, the best partners.

insights.claim: Levien concedes the NYT model is not for everyone, describing the target hire as someone obsessed with both the name on the front of the jersey and the one on the back — an explicit acceptance that individual-brand-maximizing talent will leave.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Star departures should be read as expected model output, not as institutional decay — muting the signal value of any single high-profile exit.
insights.quote: really talented people who are obsessed with both the name on the front of the jersey and the one on the back of the jersey

insights.claim: Notable recent NYT departures include columnist Ross Douthat leaving for 60 Minutes and the co-hosts of Hard Fork, including tech reporter Kevin Roose, exiting — cited by the hosts as evidence that cheap newsroom infrastructure has raised the outside option for star journalists.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Watch whether star-driven franchises (podcasts, columns) leak faster than reported news — that is where NYT's institutional model is weakest.

insights.claim: Levien is skeptical that meaningful journalism is being produced outside journalistic organizations, saying it has not been her experience as a media consumer that much of it exists — a direct pushback on the independent-creator-media thesis.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Management does not view creator platforms as a competing supply of reported journalism, so expect NYT to keep hiring institutionally rather than acquiring independent brands.
insights.quote: I will say it's not been my experience as a media consumer that you're seeing a ton of kind of journalistic work, outside of the journalistic organizations.

insights.claim: Joe Weisenthal argues the New York Times' success has made it effectively the monopsony buyer of top journalistic talent, draining roles like a Washington reporter from local outlets such as the Dallas Morning News because local papers cannot compete at internet scale.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: A structural argument that NYT's wins are non-replicable industry-wide — bearish for local news assets and for any 'NYT playbook' turnaround stories in regional media.
insights.quote: the New York Times, with its success, has become the sort of like, yeah, like the monopsony buyer of great talent in the news, business, etc.

themes.theme: Video push and its ROI question

insights.claim: Levien frames NYT video not as a substitute for reading or listening but as an attack on a separate, giant watch-native audience currently getting news-adjacent entertainment on TikTok, YouTube and Instagram — a market NYT plays in only nascently today.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: The video bet is a TAM-expansion bet, so judge it on incremental new-audience reach rather than on engagement cannibalized from existing subscribers.
insights.quote: this is not a replacement behavior for reading and listening. This is the times making a big moves into a market that we play in only in a nascent way today

insights.claim: Levien's format thesis from print-to-digital, web-to-mobile and the audio transition is that the old format never goes away — readers keep reading and listeners keep listening — so new formats add audience rather than replacing it.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: A reusable model for forecasting media format transitions: additive layering, not substitution, which argues against writing off legacy formats too early.
insights.quote: it has been our experience that the the old format does not go away. If you listen, you're going to listen.

insights.claim: Levien, who ran NYT's commercial business during the 2010s pivot to video, calls that era a cynical attempt to capture Facebook ad dollars, and distinguishes today's push as engagement-driven — targeting millions of people engaging daily rather than ad impressions.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: The test for whether this video cycle differs from the last is whether it converts to subscriptions and habit, not whether it sells video ad inventory.
insights.quote: I ran our commercial business the when the pivot to video happened, that was a cynical attempt to get ad dollars without regard to the thing I said at the very beginning, which is, can you get millions of people to engage with the thing?

insights.claim: NYT is staffing its video expansion largely from existing employees and adding capability later, which limits the incremental cost of the video build relative to a hire-first approach.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Directly relevant to the margin worry driving the post-earnings selloff: video opex should scale more slowly than video output.
insights.quote: The push and video we're making now, we are making it is largely with people who were already at the times. We're adding capability later

insights.claim: Joe Weisenthal notes the NYT stock has sold off after each of the last two earnings reports, including the one the day before this interview, on anxiety about costly video production — an investor concern Levien answers by invoking the long-game benefit of family control rather than by quantifying video ROI.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Management declined to give a video payback framework, so the cost-versus-audience debate stays unresolved into the next print — a repeatable post-earnings volatility setup.

insights.claim: Levien says newsroom resistance to on-camera work has collapsed compared with past NYT change efforts, and that putting reporters on camera explaining how they got a story is trust-building because it shows the receipts of the reporting process.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Process transparency is being used as a differentiated product feature against AI slop — a cheap, scalable trust moat competitors can copy but AI-generated content cannot.
insights.quote: This is a moment where I think people are so excited that the times is leaning in, in a really robust way to a new format.

themes.theme: Capital allocation, family control, and M&A discipline

insights.claim: Levien insists hard news journalism is NYT's most economically value-creating product 'writ large' and explicitly rejects the widespread view that serious news is a loss leader subsidized by games and sports.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: If true, NYT's earnings quality is more durable than a games-carries-news reading implies; if the claim is directional rather than accounting, segment-level disclosure is where to test it.
insights.quote: sort of hard core independent news journalism, particularly about serious topics, is like a loss leader. You do it because you have to do it. You do it for the mission.

insights.claim: Coverage spending decisions at NYT are made by editors, often below the executive editor level — the international editor decided to keep roughly 70 people in and out of Ukraine last year, five years into the war — with the CEO's job defined as making the company profitable enough that no editor has to weigh cost.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Editorial cost is structurally uncapped by design, so margin expansion at NYT must come from revenue growth rather than from newsroom cost discipline.
insights.quote: who gets to decide how many people we have on the ground in Ukraine. I think we had 70 last year in and out.

insights.claim: Levien attributes NYT's ability to make large, slow-maturing bets to the family control structure, which exists for two stated reasons: keeping journalism independent even of the company's own commercial interest, and enabling a long game.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Dual-class control is the explicit reason management can absorb post-earnings selloffs — investors buying NYT are buying a structure that will not respond to quarterly pressure.
insights.quote: Why does that control structure exist? Two reasons. One, keep the journalism independent and in service to nobody's interest, not even our own commercial interest. And two, it allows us to play long game.

insights.claim: Levien does not rule out another acquisition on the scale of The Athletic but says the return-on-investment bar for inorganic additions is 'really high,' signaling a strong preference for building in-house.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Lowers the probability of a large near-term NYT acquisition and supports a capital-return or organic-investment base case.
insights.quote: I would say to, people who think about our economics listening. The bar is really high for return on investment.

insights.claim: The Athletic integration went far better than expected culturally: NYT acquired roughly 450 journalists with only a tiny business team, has grown that newsroom by about 100 people, added a substantial editing layer it lacked, and kept it operating as an independent brand under publisher David Perpich.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: A concrete integration playbook — buy the newsroom, keep the brand separate, layer on editing and business infrastructure — that lowers execution risk on any future NYT acquisition.
insights.quote: we acquired like a giant newsroom with a tiny little business team, which was super interesting

insights.claim: NYT's games franchise is mostly organic: Wordle was acquired for materially less than The Athletic and every other game was built in-house, evidence that the highest-return product expansions came from building rather than buying.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Supports valuing NYT's product engine rather than its M&A pipeline; organic builds carry the better historical ROI record.

insights.claim: Levien states that growth in any media business is first and always a function of growing, sustaining and re-growing the engaged audience for the work — the single organizing framework she says 13 years across three media companies taught her.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Explains why NYT optimizes for engaged-audience metrics over near-term ARPU or ad yield; engagement deceleration would precede any revenue deceleration.
insights.quote: how and how much you can grow your media business is like, first and always, a question of how and how much you can grow the engaged audience for your work

themes.theme: Audience capture, trust, and newsroom control

insights.claim: Levien flatly rejects audience capture as a business model, saying NYT wants a giant engaged audience but will not chase one, and argues the total NYT audience already reflects the population at large more than the liberal stereotype implies.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Management's growth math assumes political breadth; if subscriber growth concentrates ideologically, the TAM story shrinks materially.
insights.quote: We do not chase audiences. We want a giant audience. We want a giant, engaged audience.

insights.claim: Levien extends the no-capture principle to commercial content, saying Wirecutter will name the most comfortable mattress even when a different mattress company is a big advertiser — treating advertiser-independent reviews as the source of the vertical's value.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Trust-first affiliate/review economics is the model NYT is defending against AI-generated review slop; expect no shift toward advertiser-influenced commerce content.
insights.quote: if the mattress everybody thinks is better or cooler isn't the one that our testers say is most comfortable, we're going to say the truth about that, too, even if that other mattress company is the big advertiser

insights.claim: Levien argues verified provenance is the emerging consumer demand in an environment saturated with slop and disinformation — people want to know what they receive is true, that a fair process produced it, and to see the receipts.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Positions verified-provenance journalism as a countercyclical asset whose value rises with AI content volume — the central bull case for premium news brands.
insights.quote: People want to know the thing that I'm getting is true. They want to know that a fair process was pursued to get that truth. They'd like to see the receipts of that process.

insights.claim: To manage internal ideological capture after episodes like the Tom Cotton op-ed backlash and Bari Weiss's departure, NYT built what Levien calls the largest trust and standards team in the industry, much bigger than five or six years ago, plus monthly all-company meetings that did not exist before her tenure.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: Institutional overhead is being spent specifically to prevent staff-driven editorial capture — a real cost line that also protects the trust asset the whole subscription model rests on.
insights.quote: We have a trust and standards team that is absolutely the largest in the industry.

insights.claim: NYT is funding talent-supply development it does not own, including a local investigative journalism fellowship placing people in Mississippi, Baltimore and elsewhere, to grow the pipeline of journalists trained to its independence standard.
insights.speaker: Meredith Kopit Levien
insights.so_what: A cheap hedge against the talent-monopsony problem the hosts describe, and a source of future hiring optionality outside coastal newsrooms.

insights.claim: The hosts conclude there may be room for only one bundled 'one-stop shop' in English-language media, and that the open question is how durable and how large the educated, curious, open-minded cohort is before it splinters into ideologically or personally satisfying niches.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal and Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Frames the key long-term NYT risk as cohort durability rather than competition — watch net adds among younger, vertical-native consumers for the first evidence of splintering.
insights.quote: it may be that there's only room for like one, one stop shop for content
